text: Every run ends in one of three outcomes, stated for the sources that were searched. Sufficient: the data allowed a test, so there is a verdict. Partly sufficient: only a narrower question could be tested, so the original question gets no verdict. Insufficient: no valid test could be run, so the output is a gap report.

The query asked to use whatever data are available, and the data were below the usual minimums. The test is valid, but the result rests on little data and should be read as a first look, not a conclusion.
The plan for this run was supplied in advance instead of being written by the Planner. Fixed plans are used for reference tests, where the result must be reproducible to the last digit.

Before any data are collected, the plan is fixed: the model, the scope, and the rules for excluding records. After this point nobody, agent or person, can change the rules for this run. This prevents choosing rules that produce a wanted result.

After the records have been collected and the locked rules applied, the exact set of records to be analysed is fixed and fingerprinted. Results are computed only after this point, so no record can be added or removed in response to a result.
The numbers behind the verdict, computed by code, not written by a language model. Read it to judge how strong the result is and how much data it rests on.

The fitted size of the effect, followed by its uncertainty (±, one standard error). A coefficient several times larger than its uncertainty is well determined; one about the same size as its uncertainty is not.

How the estimate was judged against the claim. The p-value is the chance of seeing an estimate this large if there were truly no effect; below the threshold it is called significant. Degrees of freedom reflect how many independent groups of data stand behind it.

Two checks that must pass before any verdict. Can a coefficient be fitted at all? Are there enough independent groups to estimate its uncertainty? If the second fails, only the coefficient is shown, with no uncertainty and no verdict.

How many records, alloys and independent groups entered the test. A group is usually one paper; records from the same paper tend to share errors, so the number of groups matters more than the number of records.
The rule, chosen when the query was written, for how much data is enough to run the test. It is fixed at the rules lock and cannot be changed after a result is seen.

The same test repeated on alternative sets of records, for example with no exclusions. If the answer changes, the result depends on those choices. Sensitivity results are shown beside the verdict and never change it.
The same test run on each source alone. These are descriptive; the pooled test gives the verdict.
Further details recorded by code for this run.

A check of how the test behaves on simulated outcomes with this dataset's structure, under stated assumptions. In a simulated world with no effect, a well-behaved test should be significant about 5% of the time. Each rate is shown with a 95% interval, because it comes from a finite number of simulations. It does not check the real data for errors.
Each point is one record. The line is the fitted relationship. Marker shapes distinguish the sources, and crosses mark records used only in a sensitivity analysis.

term: Each source alone, and all together
text: The pooled row gives the verdict. Each source row shows what that source says alone and how it compares: agrees, differs, not enough data, or no verdict when its uncertainty cannot be computed. A pooled result close to one source does not mean the sources agree.
Measured: from an experiment. Computed: from a calculation or simulation. Model-recalled: supplied by a language model from memory; shown for comparison only and never counted in the verdict.

Remarks on the result written by a separate language model after the verdict was final. It is not evidence and not the verdict. Its numbers are checked against the run record; its interpretation is not verified.

The four steps of the pipeline. Each shows what the agent received, what it returned and what it called. The Planner and the Critic never see outcome values; code, not an agent, decides which records are included and what the verdict is.

Every record found is kept, and each is placed in a group: used in the test; not eligible under the model; excluded by a rule in the plan; used only in a sensitivity analysis; or flagged by code as a duplicate, conflict or invalid value.
Tokens are the units of text a language model reads and writes. The cost is what the provider charged for this run, added up over every model call.
Editing a query creates a new version; earlier versions and their results are kept unchanged. Each dispatch of a version is a run.
A workbook with the records used, the records not used and why, the significance record, and a summary of the run, for analysis outside the site.
The scientific topic of the query, chosen from a fixed list. It selects the fields, units, checks and default rules that apply. Queries in a domain that is not yet supported cannot be dispatched.
Where the system will look. Each source is tested alone and then all together. Model recall is a comparison only and never counts toward the verdict.

Fixed minimum: the test runs only if stated minimums of records, alloys, papers and degrees of freedom are met. Power-based: gives an estimated power under stated assumptions; under review. Use what is available: tests any data that pass the validity checks and labels the result exploratory.
State one claim in plain words, naming the materials, the property and the conditions. The Planner turns it into a testable plan; it does not change what you asked.

Draft: not yet submitted. Submitted: waiting for review. Returned: sent back for edits. Dispatched or Running: in the queue or in progress. Completed: finished, with an outcome. Failed: stopped, with a reason; it can be dispatched again as a new run.
Every hypothesis ever entered, newest first, with its status, outcome and cost.
A person checks each submitted query before it runs. Dispatch sends it to the run queue; Return sends it back to be edited. Nothing runs without this step.
The most a single run may cost. A run that reaches it stops and is marked failed with that reason. A monthly cap blocks new dispatches once reached.
Runs execute one at a time, in order of dispatch. You can close the browser; the run continues.
All queries for this screen, newest first. Search by number or words, or filter by status or domain.
The five roles played by language models. Four work in the pipeline; the Commentator comments on the finished result. Each page shows the settings in use.
What a role receives, returns, may call and may not do. These are enforced by the software and cannot be changed from this page, so that the safeguards cannot be switched off by accident.
Each change to a role's settings creates a new numbered version. Every run records the versions it used, so it can be reproduced.
The sources the system can search, with their licence and kind of data.
The piece of code that reads a source and converts its records to the common format. A source can be switched on only when its adapter is ready and the connection test passes.
Reads a few records from the source and shows them in the common format, so that you can check the adapter before switching the source on.
The caps in force, and the cost and tokens used this month.

How far the data in the sources searched could take the question, from 1 to 6, set by code from the result: 6 a tested answer with a verdict; 5 an exploratory answer, with a minimum missed; 4 a coefficient only, without a valid uncertainty; 3 data found but below the minimums; 2 no coefficient could be fitted; 1 nothing tested. It describes the evidence, not whether the claim is true, and it never changes the verdict, which is shown beside the dial. A hatched dial marks a test run on constructed data.

When the plan comes from a language model's reading of the claim, the run waits before the rules lock until a named person checks what will be tested: the scope, the outcome, the exclusion rules and the minimums. The confirmation records the name, the time and exactly the text shown; if anything changed since the page was opened, it is refused and the page must be opened again. Confirming shows that a person saw the reading, not that it is right.
